lessons.title: What is AI? A practical introduction
lessons.description: A clear starting point for understanding AI, machine learning, and deep learning.
objectives: Distinguish AI, ML, and deep learning
Choose a sensible first AI use case
explanation: Artificial intelligence is an umbrella term for systems that perform tasks such as recognizing patterns, making predictions, or generating language. A system can use hand-written rules or learn from examples. Calling a product AI does not tell you whether it learns or whether its answers are reliable.

Machine learning fits a model to examples instead of requiring a developer to specify every rule. Deep learning is a family of machine-learning methods built from layered neural networks. These are nested ideas: deep learning belongs to ML, and ML belongs to AI.

Start with the task, not the technology. A fixed tax calculation is better expressed as deterministic rules. Sorting thousands of support requests may benefit from a learned classifier. In either case, decide how a person will detect and correct a bad result.

terms.definition: A representation used to produce predictions or outputs.
Adjusting a model using examples.
Using a trained model on new input.

lessons.example: A help desk receives messages about billing and technical problems. Begin with 100 human-labeled examples, define the two labels, and compare a simple keyword rule against a model on unseen messages. Keep ambiguous requests in a human review queue.
mistakes: Confusing fluent language with factual understanding.
Choosing AI before checking whether a simple rule solves the problem.
Assuming performance on examples guarantees future performance.
lessons.exercise: List three tasks from your work. For each, choose rules, ML, or human judgment and explain the cost of one wrong decision.

questions.question: Is all AI machine learning?
questions.answer: No. Rule-based systems can be AI without learning from data. ML is one approach inside the broader field.

questions.question: What is inference in the help-desk example?

options: Assigning a category to a new message using an already trained model; it does not require retraining.

questions.answer: Deep learning uses layered neural networks and is a subset of machine learning, not a synonym for all AI.
options: Deep learning uses layered neural networks and is a subset of machine learning, not a synonym for all AI.

lessons.title: Capabilities, limitations & responsible AI
lessons.description: Know where AI helps, where it fails, and who stays accountable.
objectives: Recognize plausible but unsupported outputs
Design an escalation and review process
explanation: AI systems can compress information, classify examples, and produce useful drafts, but their outputs need a purpose-specific standard of correctness. A persuasive answer is not evidence. Errors can arise from missing context, poor examples, distribution changes, or the limits of the method itself.

Responsible use begins with people affected by the system. Identify the decision owner, the potential harm, and a route to appeal. Measure performance for relevant groups and situations rather than reporting one average. A system that works well overall may fail badly for a small group.

Use a risk register as a living design artifact. Write the failure, its impact, its owner, and a mitigation that can be checked. A human-review label is meaningful only if reviewers have time, evidence, authority, and a way to override the output.

terms.definition: An output that appears credible but lacks factual support.
A change between development data and real use.
A practical way for people to review and intervene.

lessons.example: For an internal policy assistant, require links to approved policies, display the document date, and route unanswered questions to HR. Audit a sample of answers weekly. Do not permit the assistant to make employment decisions.
mistakes: Treating a disclaimer as a complete mitigation.
Testing only easy or frequent cases.
Giving reviewers no access to the evidence.
lessons.exercise: Create a risk register for a support assistant with three failures, named owners, mitigations, and a test for each.

questions.question: Does confident wording prove an AI answer is correct?
questions.answer: No. Fluency and correctness are different properties. Check important claims against evidence appropriate to the task.
options: No. Fluency and correctness are different properties. Check important claims against evidence appropriate to the task.
Yes, confidence in wording reflects verified facts.

questions.question: What makes human review effective?
questions.answer: Reviewers need evidence, time, authority, and a clear override route; merely showing a confirmation button is insufficient.
options: A reviewer clicking approve on every output.
Reviewers need evidence, time, authority, and a clear override route; merely showing a confirmation button is insufficient.

questions.question: A model fails on a new customer group. What next?
questions.answer: Inspect representative examples and group-specific metrics, constrain use if needed, and evaluate fixes before expanding access.
options: Inspect representative examples and group-specific metrics, constrain use if needed, and evaluate fixes before expanding access.
Keep using the overall accuracy score.

questions.question: Who owns an AI-assisted decision?
questions.answer: An accountable person or organization must own the decision and its consequences; the model cannot take responsibility.
options: The model becomes legally and operationally responsible.
An accountable person or organization must own the decision and its consequences; the model cannot take responsibility.

questions.question: What belongs in a risk register?
questions.answer: A concrete failure, affected people, likelihood or exposure, impact, owner, mitigation, and verification plan.
options: A concrete failure, affected people, likelihood or exposure, impact, owner, mitigation, and verification plan.
Only a list of model names.

lessons.title: AI in everyday decisions
lessons.description: Separate a useful prediction from the decision it helps a person make.
objectives: Identify predictions inside familiar products
Choose a useful baseline and a human review point
explanation: An email filter predicts whether a message resembles spam. A recommendation system ranks items you may prefer. In both cases, a prediction is only one part of a product: someone also chooses the action, the error tolerance, and the way users can correct mistakes.

Start with the decision. Who uses the output, what information is available at that moment, and what happens when the system is wrong? Compare the AI approach with a simple rule or the existing manual process. A model that scores well but creates more review work may not improve the task.

Match oversight to consequences. Sorting a playlist is easy to undo; blocking an important message needs a visible recovery route. Test realistic exceptions, record corrections, and revisit performance when users or inputs change. A fluent explanation does not establish that a prediction is correct.

terms.definition: An estimate made from available inputs.
A reference approach used to judge an improvement.
Accepting a system output too readily because it appears authoritative.

lessons.example: A fictional team receives 200 emails per day. Its filter catches 30 unwanted messages but hides two customer requests. Compare time saved with time spent reviewing the spam folder. Offer restore and report-error controls before increasing automation.
mistakes: Measuring prediction accuracy without considering the resulting action.
Calling every rule-based feature machine learning.
Removing a correction route because a demo looked convincing.
lessons.exercise: Choose a recommendation, search, or spam feature. Write its input, prediction, action, baseline, one costly mistake, and one way a user can recover. Decide which metric would show a useful improvement.

questions.question: Is a spam prediction the same as deleting a message?
questions.answer: No. Prediction estimates a label; deletion is an application decision with separate consequences.
options: Yes, classification always requires deletion.
No. Prediction estimates a label; deletion is an application decision with separate consequences.

questions.question: What baseline fits a new email-priority model?
questions.answer: Compare it with the current manual process or a simple sender rule on the same messages.
options: Compare it with the current manual process or a simple sender rule on the same messages.

questions.question: A filter saves time but hides urgent requests. What should change?
questions.answer: Measure missed urgent messages and improve review or recovery before expanding automation.
options: Remove the review folder to make the process faster.
Measure missed urgent messages and improve review or recovery before expanding automation.

questions.question: How would you explain an AI feature without jargon?
questions.answer: Name the input, the estimate it produces, who uses it, and how mistakes are corrected.

questions.question: What evidence supports keeping a recommendation feature?

A measured improvement in the intended user outcome, with acceptable errors and effort.

lessons.title: A glossary of AI terminology
lessons.description: Connect the vocabulary of data, models, training, and inference.
objectives: Distinguish data, parameters, and prompts
Explain training and inference with one example
explanation: A dataset contains examples. A feature describes an input; a label records the target in supervised learning. A model uses learned parameters to map inputs to outputs. Training adjusts those parameters, while inference applies the trained model to new inputs.

Generative applications add another vocabulary layer. A token is a unit processed by a model, and a prompt is input supplied for a particular request. An embedding represents an item as numbers useful for comparison. A context window limits how much information a request can contain.

Keep quality terms precise. A benchmark is a defined test collection; an evaluation is the process of measuring behavior. A hallucination is unsupported generated content, not simply any disliked answer. Retrieval supplies external information at request time; it does not itself update model weights.

terms.definition: A value adjusted during model training.
Applying a trained model to an input.
A numerical representation used for tasks such as similarity search.

lessons.example: For a fictional support classifier, message text is input and billing is a label. Training learns from labeled messages. Classifying a new message is inference. Adding an instruction to return JSON changes the prompt, not automatically the learned parameters.
mistakes: Using token and word as exact synonyms.
Calling every prompt edit fine-tuning.
Treating a benchmark score as a guarantee for a different task.
lessons.exercise: Draw a five-box diagram from raw examples to training, saved model, new request, and output. Label where parameters change and where retrieved context could be added. Explain the diagram to someone unfamiliar with AI.

questions.question: Does editing a prompt necessarily retrain a model?
questions.answer: No. A prompt changes request context; training changes learned parameters.
options: No. A prompt changes request context; training changes learned parameters.
Yes, every request permanently updates the weights.

questions.question: Which item is a label in a spam dataset?
questions.answer: The expected spam or not-spam category associated with a message.
options: The font used to display the message.
The expected spam or not-spam category associated with a message.

questions.question: A chatbot retrieves a policy. Has it fine-tuned itself?
questions.answer: No. Retrieval adds context for the request without itself changing model weights.
options: No. Retrieval adds context for the request without itself changing model weights.
Yes, retrieving any document is weight training.

questions.question: How do training and inference differ?
questions.answer: Training adjusts parameters using examples; inference uses parameters to produce an output.
options: Inference always requires labeled examples and changes every weight.
Training adjusts parameters using examples; inference uses parameters to produce an output.

questions.question: Can a token count be replaced with a word count?
questions.answer: No. Tokenization varies, so use the chosen model tokenizer or reported usage.
options: No. Tokenization varies, so use the chosen model tokenizer or reported usage.
Yes, every language has exactly one token per word.

lessons.title: Python essentials for working with data
lessons.description: Use lists, dictionaries, and simple validation to prepare useful examples.
lessons.prerequisites: Basic familiarity with files and a terminal.
objectives: Transform records with Python
Handle missing values deliberately
explanation: A data pipeline is a sequence of small transformations. In Python, a list keeps an ordered collection and a dictionary maps keys to values. A list of dictionaries is a convenient starting point for small datasets, because each record can hold named fields.

Before computing anything, inspect the shape and meaning of the data. Is a missing score unknown, zero, or invalid? Those meanings are different. Avoid silently turning unknown values into zeros, because that changes the statistics and can teach a model the wrong pattern.

Keep cleaning rules explicit and preserve the original input. Use small examples to check edge cases before processing a whole dataset. As volume grows, a database or dataframe may be more appropriate, but validation and traceability still matter.

terms.definition: A collection of fields describing one example.
An absent or unknown measurement.
A compact expression for constructing a collection.

lessons.example: The Python 3 snippet filters unknown scores before calculating an average. With scores 2 and 4, the result is 3.0. An empty valid list produces None instead of division by zero.

code.title: Average only the known scores
code.source:
records = [{"score": 2}, {"score": None}, {"score": 4}]
scores = [r["score"] for r in records if r["score"] is not None]
average = sum(scores) / len(scores) if scores else None
print(average)  # 3.0

mistakes: Using zero for every missing value.
Mutating the only copy of raw data.
Dividing by the length of the unfiltered dataset.
lessons.exercise: Add a record with score 0 and one with score None. Predict the average, run the snippet locally, and explain why zero must remain.

questions.question: Why use a dictionary for a record?
questions.answer: Named keys make fields explicit, so code can access a score without depending on a fragile numeric position.
options: Named keys make fields explicit, so code can access a score without depending on a fragile numeric position.
A dictionary automatically validates every field.

questions.question: Should a valid zero score be filtered out?
questions.answer: No. Zero is a measured value; filter specifically for None when None represents missingness.
options: Yes, because zero always means missing.
No. Zero is a measured value; filter specifically for None when None represents missingness.

questions.question: What should the average of no valid scores be?
questions.answer: Return an explicit missing result or raise a documented error; dividing by zero or inventing an average hides the problem.
options: Return an explicit missing result or raise a documented error; dividing by zero or inventing an average hides the problem.
Always return the last record.

questions.question: Why preserve raw input data?
questions.answer: It lets you reproduce results, audit cleaning decisions, and rerun a corrected transformation without losing information.
options: It makes every algorithm unbiased.
It lets you reproduce results, audit cleaning decisions, and rerun a corrected transformation without losing information.

questions.question: When might lists become insufficient?
questions.answer: Large datasets, joins, and concurrent access often call for databases or dataframe tools; use the workload to choose.
options: Large datasets, joins, and concurrent access often call for databases or dataframe tools; use the workload to choose.
Lists cannot hold more than ten records.

lessons.title: SQL for AI practitioners
lessons.description: Select, join, and aggregate records without changing their meaning.
lessons.prerequisites: Python essentials for working with data.
objectives: Build a parameterized query
Check row counts and missing values before using a dataset
explanation: SQL describes which records you want from tables. SELECT chooses fields, WHERE filters rows, and GROUP BY creates groups for aggregates. Begin by defining what one row represents. A ticket table and a ticket-events table have different granularities, even if both contain ticket IDs.

A join combines matching rows. If one ticket has four events, joining tickets to events produces four rows for that ticket. Count distinct tickets or aggregate events first when your analysis needs one row per ticket. Use IS NULL to inspect missing values; SQL NULL is not the same as zero.

Bind user-supplied values through query parameters instead of joining them into SQL text. Parameters protect values; they do not choose safe table names or grant permissions. Keep extraction accounts read-only when possible and document the query, snapshot date, and filters used for a training dataset.

terms.definition: Combining rows according to matching keys.
Summarizing multiple rows with operations such as COUNT or AVG.
Passing values separately from SQL command text.

lessons.example: The SQLite example groups invented ticket scores by team. The NULL score is excluded from AVG, and a parameter limits the query to one team. Check the result count before interpreting a team average as representative.
mistakes: Counting joined event rows as distinct customers.
Concatenating a search string into SQL.
Treating NULL as a measured zero.
lessons.exercise: Run sql_summary.py. Add another score and an unknown score to the invented records. Predict AVG and COUNT(score), then compare them with COUNT(*). Explain which count answers each question.

code.title: Aggregate invented ticket scores
code.source:
import sqlite3

with sqlite3.connect(':memory:') as connection:
    connection.execute('CREATE TABLE scores (team TEXT, score REAL)')
    connection.executemany('INSERT INTO scores VALUES (?, ?)', [
        ('support', 3), ('support', 5), ('support', None), ('sales', 2)
    ])
    row = connection.execute(
        'SELECT team, AVG(score), COUNT(score), COUNT(*) '
        'FROM scores WHERE team = ? GROUP BY team', ('support',)
    ).fetchone()
    print(f'{row[0]}: average={row[1]:.1f}, known={row[2]}, rows={row[3]}')

questions.question: Why define table granularity before a join?
questions.answer: It tells you whether a join multiplies entities and changes the meaning of later counts.
options: It tells you whether a join multiplies entities and changes the meaning of later counts.
It guarantees every key occurs only once.

questions.question: How should a team name enter a SQL query?
questions.answer: Bind it as a query parameter rather than interpolating it into SQL text.
options: Append it directly after the WHERE keyword.
Bind it as a query parameter rather than interpolating it into SQL text.

questions.question: One ticket joins to three events. How many joined rows can result?
questions.answer: Three; use a suitable aggregation when you need one record per ticket.
options: Three; use a suitable aggregation when you need one record per ticket.
Exactly one because SQL automatically deduplicates entities.

questions.question: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(score)?
questions.answer: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(score) counts rows where score is not NULL.
options: Both always ignore rows containing any NULL field.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(score) counts rows where score is not NULL.

questions.question: Does parameter binding authorize access to a table?
questions.answer: No. The database identity still needs appropriate access permissions.
options: No. The database identity still needs appropriate access permissions.
Yes, binding a value grants read access automatically.

lessons.title: Git and reproducible experiments
lessons.description: Record enough context to understand and repeat an experiment.
objectives: Review and commit a focused change
Connect a result to code, data, and configuration versions
explanation: Git records snapshots of tracked files. The working tree holds your current edits; the staging area selects what goes into the next commit. Use git status and git diff to inspect changes, then stage named files and inspect git diff --cached before committing.

A commit alone does not reproduce an AI experiment. Also record a data version or content hash, dependency versions, model identifier, configuration, evaluation cases, and random seeds where supported. External services and hardware can introduce variation even with the same seed.

Keep secrets, private datasets, generated caches, and large model files out of ordinary source commits. An ignore rule prevents accidental addition of untracked files; it does not remove files already tracked or erase history. Store a small experiment manifest beside a measured result so someone else can identify its inputs.

terms.definition: A recorded snapshot linked to repository history.
The selected changes prepared for the next commit.
A record of the inputs and settings needed to identify an experiment.

lessons.example: Experiment E12 compares two chunk sizes on the same ten questions. Its manifest records the code commit, document snapshot hash, embedding model version, chunk settings, and metrics. A changed source document becomes a new experiment input even if the code stays unchanged.
mistakes: Committing credentials with experiment settings.
Assuming a seed controls a remote service.
Keeping results without identifying the input dataset.
lessons.exercise: Create a small local repository with a script and an experiment manifest. Make one change, inspect the staged diff, and commit it. Write what another person would still need to reproduce the output.

questions.question: What does the Git staging area control?
questions.answer: It selects the changes included in the next commit.
options: It selects the changes included in the next commit.
It automatically backs up every file on the computer.

questions.question: Which command reviews changes selected for a commit?
questions.answer: git diff --cached shows the staged changes before committing.
options: git push displays only unstaged changes.
git diff --cached shows the staged changes before committing.

questions.question: A model alias changes behind the same name. Is the experiment fully pinned?
questions.answer: No. Record a resolved model version or acknowledge that the provider can change it.
options: No. Record a resolved model version or acknowledge that the provider can change it.
Yes, a name always identifies immutable weights.

questions.question: Why is a commit insufficient for experiment reproducibility?
questions.answer: Data, dependencies, configuration, external models, and environment can also affect results.
options: Code cannot influence AI experiment results.
Data, dependencies, configuration, external models, and environment can also affect results.

questions.question: Will adding a tracked secret to .gitignore erase it from history?
questions.answer: No. Revoke the credential and follow an appropriate repository cleanup procedure.
options: No. Revoke the credential and follow an appropriate repository cleanup procedure.
Yes, ignore rules rewrite all prior commits.

lessons.title: Statistics and probability for AI
lessons.description: Use summaries, denominators, and base rates to interpret results.
objectives: Compare mean and median
Use a base rate when interpreting a positive prediction
explanation: A mean sums values and divides by their count. A median describes the middle of sorted observations. Both summarize data, but a few extreme values can move the mean substantially. Always report the population, units, sample size, and missing-value treatment with a summary.

Probability describes uncertainty under stated assumptions. Conditional probability restricts attention to cases satisfying a condition. The chance a flagged item is truly positive depends on how common positives were before the test, as well as on the test errors. Sensitivity alone cannot answer that question.

Suppose 10 of 1,000 invented items are faulty. A detector catches 9 faulty items and falsely flags 99 good ones. Only 9 of 108 flags are real faults, about 8.3%. Check such counts before deciding whether a system can act automatically. A tiny evaluation sample also leaves substantial uncertainty about future performance.

terms.definition: Sum of observed values divided by their count.
The middle value, or average of the two middle values, after sorting.
How common an outcome is in the relevant population.

lessons.example: Four response times are 1, 1, 2, and 20 seconds. Their mean is 6 seconds and median is 1.5 seconds. Neither alone describes the slowest user experience, so also inspect the distribution and slow cases.
mistakes: Reporting a percentage without its denominator.
Assuming a small sample represents all users.
Confusing the chance of a flag given a fault with the chance of a fault given a flag.
lessons.exercise: Run summary_statistics.py. Replace the 20-second outlier with 2 seconds and predict the new mean and median. For the detector example, halve false positives and recompute the fraction of valid alerts.

code.title: Mean and median of response times
code.source:
from statistics import mean, median

seconds = [1, 1, 2, 20]
print(f'mean={mean(seconds):.1f}, median={median(seconds):.1f}')
true_positives, false_positives = 9, 99
precision = true_positives / (true_positives + false_positives)
print(f'precision={precision:.1%}')

questions.question: Why can latency mean and median differ greatly?
questions.answer: A small number of slow responses can raise the mean while most responses remain fast.
options: A small number of slow responses can raise the mean while most responses remain fast.
The median always includes only failed requests.

questions.question: What denominator gives precision for the detector example?
questions.answer: All flagged items: 9 true positives plus 99 false positives.
options: All 1,000 items regardless of prediction.
All flagged items: 9 true positives plus 99 false positives.

questions.question: Nine of 108 flags are real faults. What is the approximate precision?
questions.answer: 8.3%; most flags are false positives in this example.
options: 8.3%; most flags are false positives in this example.
90%, because nine of ten faults were detected.

questions.question: Why mention sample size with an accuracy estimate?
questions.answer: An estimate from few cases may be unstable and may miss important subgroups.
options: Sample size makes every dataset representative.
An estimate from few cases may be unstable and may miss important subgroups.

questions.question: Should an unknown measurement automatically become zero?
questions.answer: No. Define and report a missing-data policy appropriate to what was measured.
options: No. Define and report a missing-data policy appropriate to what was measured.
Yes, zero is always statistically neutral.

lessons.title: Linear algebra intuition
lessons.description: Read vectors, dot products, and matrix shapes in an AI pipeline.
objectives: Calculate a small dot product
Check dimensions before combining arrays
explanation: A vector is an ordered collection of numbers. It can represent measurements such as price and quantity, or a learned embedding with many dimensions. A matrix arranges numbers into rows and columns. State what each axis means before performing an operation.

The dot product multiplies corresponding vector entries and adds the results. For features [2, 3] and weights [4, 5], the result is 23. A linear prediction can add a bias afterward. For a batch with shape n by d and weights of length d, matrix multiplication produces n scores.

Magnitude and direction describe different properties. Cosine similarity divides a dot product by the product of vector lengths, comparing direction. It is undefined for a zero-length vector. Numerical closeness only becomes meaningful when vectors use a compatible representation; dimensions matching does not prove two embedding models share a coordinate system.

terms.definition: The number of coordinates in a vector or size of an array axis.
Sum of products of corresponding coordinates.
A measure of vector magnitude.

lessons.example: A toy score weights two inputs using [4, 5]. The first record [2, 3] scores 23; a second [1, 0] scores 4. These invented weights illustrate shape and arithmetic, not a trained or validated prediction model.
mistakes: Multiplying incompatible shapes.
Comparing embeddings from unrelated models.
Computing cosine similarity without handling zero vectors.
lessons.exercise: Run dot_product.py. Change the features and calculate the score by hand. Add a third feature without changing the weights and observe the validation error. Explain which axis a batch would add.

code.title: A validated dot product

questions.question: What does a vector dimension count?
questions.answer: The number of coordinates in the representation.
options: The number of models trained on the data.
The number of coordinates in the representation.

questions.question: What is the dot product of [2, 3] and [4, 5]?
questions.answer: 23, from 2 × 4 plus 3 × 5.
options: 23, from 2 × 4 plus 3 × 5.
14, from adding all four numbers.

questions.question: Can equal-length embeddings from different models be mixed safely?
questions.answer: Not automatically; their coordinates can represent different learned spaces.
options: Yes, equal dimensions guarantee identical meaning.
Not automatically; their coordinates can represent different learned spaces.

questions.question: How does cosine similarity differ from a raw dot product?
questions.answer: It normalizes by vector magnitudes to compare direction.
options: It normalizes by vector magnitudes to compare direction.
It ignores all coordinates except the largest.

questions.question: What should happen when cosine similarity receives a zero vector?
questions.answer: Handle it explicitly because division by a zero norm is undefined.
options: Return perfect similarity to every vector.
Handle it explicitly because division by a zero norm is undefined.

lessons.title: Regression, classification & clustering
lessons.description: Match the learning method to the question your data needs to answer.
objectives: Separate supervised and unsupervised tasks
Choose a baseline and evaluation metric
explanation: Supervised learning uses examples with target answers. Regression predicts a numeric quantity, such as delivery time. Classification predicts a category or a probability over categories, such as whether a transaction needs review. The target must correspond to information you will actually know after the event.

Unsupervised learning searches for structure without a supplied target for every example. Clustering groups similar items according to a chosen representation and distance. A cluster is not automatically a meaningful business segment; people need to interpret and validate it.

Choose features available at the time of prediction. A support ticket closure date cannot help predict urgency when the ticket first arrives. Establish a baseline such as the median for regression or the most frequent class for classification, then check whether the model improves a useful metric.

terms.definition: An input measurement used by a model.
The outcome a supervised model learns to predict.
Grouping examples by a chosen similarity notion.

lessons.example: For a delivery service, predicted minutes is regression; late versus on-time is classification; grouping customers by ordering patterns is clustering. Each question requires different labels and a different way to judge success.
mistakes: Including future information as a feature.
Interpreting cluster IDs as ordered scores.
Choosing accuracy for a highly imbalanced task without inspecting errors.
lessons.exercise: Write one regression, one classification, and one clustering question for an online store. List inputs available at decision time.

questions.question: Is predicting a house price classification?
questions.answer: Usually no: predicting a numeric price is regression. Predicting a price band would be classification.
options: Yes, all predictions are classifications.
Usually no: predicting a numeric price is regression. Predicting a price band would be classification.

questions.question: What target does clustering require?
questions.answer: Clustering does not require a target label per example; it groups inputs using a representation and similarity rule.
options: Clustering does not require a target label per example; it groups inputs using a representation and similarity rule.
It requires the correct cluster label for every example.

questions.question: Can ticket closure time predict initial urgency?
questions.answer: Not if closure time is unknown when urgency is assigned. That would leak future information into development.
options: Yes, any correlated column is a valid input.
Not if closure time is unknown when urgency is assigned. That would leak future information into development.

questions.question: Why start with a simple baseline?
questions.answer: It reveals whether added complexity produces a meaningful improvement over an inexpensive, understandable alternative.
options: It reveals whether added complexity produces a meaningful improvement over an inexpensive, understandable alternative.
It guarantees the final model will be linear.

questions.question: Are cluster labels 0 and 1 rankings?
questions.answer: No. Cluster identifiers are arbitrary names unless an explicit ranking is added and justified.
options: Yes, cluster 1 is always better than cluster 0.
No. Cluster identifiers are arbitrary names unless an explicit ranking is added and justified.

lessons.title: Evaluate models without fooling yourself
lessons.description: Use careful splits and error analysis to measure generalization.
objectives: Prevent leakage in preprocessing
Explain precision and recall
explanation: A model needs evaluation on examples that were not used to fit it. Separate training, validation, and final test roles. Training fits parameters; validation guides choices; the final test estimates performance after those choices are settled. Repeatedly optimizing against the test set makes it part of development.

Choose a split that resembles deployment. For future forecasting, train on earlier records and test on later ones. For patient or customer data, keep one person out of multiple splits when that would create near-duplicate examples. Fit preprocessing on training data only.

Precision asks how many positive predictions are correct; recall asks how many actual positives are found. The right trade-off depends on the cost of false alarms and missed cases. Inspect mistakes and report uncertainty rather than treating a single score as a universal guarantee.

terms.definition: Information available during development that would not legitimately be available in production.
True positives divided by predicted positives.
True positives divided by actual positives.

lessons.example: A review queue flags 20 payments; 15 are truly problematic. There are 30 problematic payments overall. Precision is 15/20 = 75%; recall is 15/30 = 50%. Improving recall may increase the reviewer workload.

code.title: Compute precision and recall
code.source:
def precision_recall(tp, fp, fn):
    precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else None
    recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else None
    return precision, recall


# 20 flagged payments, 15 correct; 30 problematic payments in total.
precision, recall = precision_recall(tp=15, fp=5, fn=15)
print(f"precision={precision:.2f} recall={recall:.2f}")

mistakes: Normalizing on the entire dataset before splitting.
Reporting only accuracy when positives are rare.
Changing the model repeatedly after inspecting the final test results.
lessons.exercise: Draw a confusion matrix for 15 true positives, 5 false positives, 15 false negatives, and 65 true negatives. Compute precision and recall.

questions.question: Why keep a final test set separate?
questions.answer: It estimates performance after model choices are fixed. Reusing it to tune choices biases the estimate.
options: It supplies extra training labels during every iteration.
It estimates performance after model choices are fixed. Reusing it to tune choices biases the estimate.

questions.question: What is precision for 15 correct flags out of 20 flags?
questions.answer: 75%, because precision divides true positives by all predicted positives.
options: 75%, because precision divides true positives by all predicted positives.
50%, because precision divides by all actual positives.

questions.question: How should a future-demand model be split?
questions.answer: Use a time-aware split that trains on earlier data and evaluates on later data, matching the intended prediction setting.
options: Always shuffle all dates randomly.
Use a time-aware split that trains on earlier data and evaluates on later data, matching the intended prediction setting.

questions.question: Why can 99% accuracy be misleading?
questions.answer: If only 1% of examples are positive, predicting negative every time reaches 99% while finding none of the positives.
options: If only 1% of examples are positive, predicting negative every time reaches 99% while finding none of the positives.
Accuracy above 90% always proves usefulness.

questions.question: Where should a scaler be fitted?
questions.answer: Fit it on training data, then apply the learned transformation to validation and test sets to avoid leakage.
options: Fit it on all data before creating splits.
Fit it on training data, then apply the learned transformation to validation and test sets to avoid leakage.

lessons.title: Feature engineering in practice
lessons.description: Create useful inputs while preventing training and evaluation leakage.
lessons.prerequisites: Machine learning problem types and model evaluation.
objectives: Choose features available at prediction time
Fit transformations on training data only
explanation: Feature engineering turns raw records into inputs that help a model solve a task. Examples include time since a previous event, a count within a past window, and a category encoding. Write down when each input becomes available; an excellent predictor that appears after the decision is leakage.

Split examples before learning preprocessing statistics. Fit imputation, scaling, vocabulary, and feature selection on the training partition, then apply the fitted transformations to validation and test partitions. A pipeline helps keep transformations attached to the model and inside each cross-validation fold.

Evaluate additions against a simple baseline. Scaling can help distance-based and regularized models; categorical encoding needs a policy for unseen values. Compare metrics and error slices after each change. Keep feature definitions shared between training and serving so the same record receives the same interpretation.

terms.definition: Using information that would not legitimately be available for the prediction.
Filling missing inputs using an explicit rule.
A mismatch between feature processing during training and use.

lessons.example: To predict whether a support request will breach a deadline, use its age at scoring time and queue size. Do not use the final resolution timestamp. Fit median replacement values on historical training records, then apply those fixed values to newer requests.
mistakes: Fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting.
Adding post-outcome fields as predictors.
Silently assigning an unseen category to an unrelated known category.
lessons.exercise: List six possible features for the support example. Mark when each becomes available. Reject leaked features, specify missing and unknown-category rules, and design a time-based comparison with the baseline.

questions.question: Why can resolution time leak information into a breach predictor?
questions.answer: It is known after the outcome, while the model must predict beforehand.
options: Every timestamp is forbidden in machine learning.
It is known after the outcome, while the model must predict beforehand.

questions.question: Where should a scaler learn its mean and variance?
questions.answer: On the training data within each evaluation fold.
options: On the training data within each evaluation fold.
On all records including the final test set.

questions.question: A new category appears in production. What is needed?
questions.answer: A documented unknown-category policy supported by the fitted transformation.
options: A new arbitrary numeric meaning on every request.
A documented unknown-category policy supported by the fitted transformation.

questions.question: What does a preprocessing pipeline help prevent?
questions.answer: Inconsistent transformations and fitting steps outside the intended training split.
options: Inconsistent transformations and fitting steps outside the intended training split.
All possible dataset bias automatically.

questions.question: How do you know a new feature helps?
questions.answer: Compare held-out performance and relevant error slices against the same baseline.
options: Count how many columns the dataset now has.
Compare held-out performance and relevant error slices against the same baseline.

lessons.title: Unsupervised learning beyond clustering
lessons.description: Explore dimensionality reduction and anomaly detection without target labels.
lessons.prerequisites: Machine learning problem types and linear algebra intuition.
objectives: Distinguish compression from clustering
Evaluate an unsupervised result against its intended use
explanation: Unsupervised methods look for structure without a supplied target for each example. Clustering groups similar items; dimensionality reduction compresses a representation; anomaly detection identifies observations unlike a reference population. These objectives do not automatically discover useful business categories.

Principal component analysis finds orthogonal directions of variation and projects data onto selected directions. Scaling affects which features dominate the result. Retaining high variance can preserve important structure, but a low-variance feature may still carry the signal needed for a downstream task.

Evaluate the intended use. For compression, inspect reconstruction error and downstream performance. For anomaly alerts, review a labeled sample and estimate analyst workload. For a two-dimensional plot, avoid interpreting distance as proof of real-world similarity. Hold out data when selecting transformations and thresholds.

terms.definition: A linear projection onto directions of variation.
Difference between an input and its reconstruction from a compressed representation.
An observation unusual relative to a chosen reference.

lessons.example: A team compresses 40 sensor measurements to six components. It checks whether a later fault detector still catches faults. Separately, an outlier detector flags unusual devices for inspection; a flag can reflect a broken sensor rather than an actual equipment fault.
mistakes: Equating unusual with harmful.
Naming clusters as if the algorithm verified their meaning.
Choosing dimensionality only because a plot looks attractive.
lessons.exercise: Design a small sensor experiment. Specify the reference population, scaling, a holdout period, one compression metric, and one downstream success metric. Describe two harmless reasons for an anomaly alert.

questions.question: Does unsupervised learning require a target label for every example?
questions.answer: No. Its training objective can use structure in the inputs themselves.
options: Yes, all unsupervised algorithms require class labels.
No. Its training objective can use structure in the inputs themselves.

questions.question: Why inspect scaling before PCA?
questions.answer: Features with larger numeric variation can dominate the selected directions.
options: Features with larger numeric variation can dominate the selected directions.
Scaling converts PCA into a supervised classifier.

questions.question: An anomaly detector flags a new device model. What should an analyst check?
questions.answer: Whether the reference distribution covers that device before treating the alert as a fault.
options: Assume novelty proves physical damage.
Whether the reference distribution covers that device before treating the alert as a fault.

questions.question: Does high explained variance guarantee predictive quality?
questions.answer: No. Preserved variance may not contain the signal needed by the downstream task.
options: No. Preserved variance may not contain the signal needed by the downstream task.
Yes, the highest-variance direction is always the target.

questions.question: How can compression be evaluated?
questions.answer: Measure reconstruction and the performance of the downstream task on held-out data.
options: Check only the number of colors in a plot.
Measure reconstruction and the performance of the downstream task on held-out data.

lessons.title: Neural networks, embeddings & transformers
lessons.description: Build an intuitive map of modern deep learning.
lessons.prerequisites: Basic vectors and the idea of training.
objectives: Explain learned representations
Describe attention without assuming understanding
explanation: A neural network transforms numeric inputs through layers with learned weights. During training, a loss measures the mismatch between output and target, and an optimizer adjusts weights to reduce that loss. More layers do not automatically make a system more useful; data, objectives, and evaluation matter.

An embedding represents an item as a vector. Useful embeddings place task-relevant items near one another under a chosen similarity measure. The representation is learned, so nearby vectors reflect training patterns rather than an objective definition of meaning.

Transformers use attention to mix information across positions. This helps a representation depend on surrounding context. In text, the same word can be represented differently in different sentences. Vision and multimodal systems can also process sequences of image patches or other representations. Architecture alone does not ensure truth, fairness, or reasoning reliability.

terms.definition: A learned numeric parameter.
A measure of mismatch used for optimization.
A numeric vector representing an item.
A mechanism for combining information across positions.

lessons.example: In a document search system, embed a question and candidate paragraphs, compare their vectors, and inspect the nearest results. Try the ambiguous word bank in two full sentences and notice why context matters.
mistakes: Treating vector similarity as proof of factual agreement.
Assuming larger networks always improve a specific task.
Mixing vectors from incompatible embedding models.
lessons.exercise: Sketch a pipeline from text to tokens to vectors to prediction. Annotate what is learned during training and what runs during inference.

questions.question: What does training adjust in a neural network?
questions.answer: It adjusts parameters such as weights to reduce a training objective; it does not manually write one rule per example.
options: It adjusts parameters such as weights to reduce a training objective; it does not manually write one rule per example.
It changes only the spelling of labels.

questions.question: What is an embedding used for?
questions.answer: It gives items numeric representations that can support similarity search and downstream learning.
options: It is always a compressed copy of the original document.
It gives items numeric representations that can support similarity search and downstream learning.

questions.question: Can vectors from unrelated embedding models be compared directly?
questions.answer: Usually not meaningfully: their coordinates and dimensions may represent different spaces. Use a compatible model consistently.
options: Usually not meaningfully: their coordinates and dimensions may represent different spaces. Use a compatible model consistently.
Yes, all embedding coordinates have universal meanings.

questions.question: What does attention contribute?
questions.answer: It allows information from different positions to influence a representation, making outputs sensitive to context.
options: It certifies every generated statement as true.
It allows information from different positions to influence a representation, making outputs sensitive to context.

questions.question: Does high semantic similarity guarantee agreement?
questions.answer: No. Opposing claims about the same topic can be similar; check the content before using a retrieved passage as evidence.
options: No. Opposing claims about the same topic can be similar; check the content before using a retrieved passage as evidence.
Yes, similar vectors always express the same fact.

lessons.title: Introduction to computer vision
lessons.description: Choose an image task and build an evaluation that reflects real use.
objectives: Distinguish classification, detection, and segmentation
Design a transfer-learning baseline without image leakage
explanation: Computer vision transforms images into outputs for a task. Classification assigns labels to an image. Detection adds object locations, usually boxes. Segmentation assigns labels to pixels. Choose the output required by the user before selecting a model or collecting annotations.

Transfer learning starts with a model trained elsewhere. You can freeze a feature extractor and train a new head, or fine-tune selected layers. Keep resize, channel order, and normalization consistent with the chosen model. Apply random augmentation to training images, while evaluation preprocessing should be repeatable.

Split by the source of correlated images. Adjacent video frames, repeated photos of the same object, or one camera session can leak across a random split. Evaluate lighting, viewpoint, background, and device differences. A model can exploit a label watermark instead of learning the intended object.

terms.definition: Predicting object categories and locations.
Assigning a category to individual pixels.
Adapting representations learned from another training task.

lessons.example: A fictional packaging inspection project needs the location of torn labels, so image-level classification alone is insufficient. Keep all photos of a package in one partition and include a separate lighting setup in the evaluation.
mistakes: Splitting neighboring video frames randomly.
Changing image normalization between training and inference.
Treating a confidence score as a calibrated probability without checking.
lessons.exercise: Define an inspection task with five invented image descriptions. Choose the annotation type, group-based split, two realistic augmentations, and a failure review plan. Explain what image-level accuracy would miss.

questions.question: Which output distinguishes detection from image classification?
questions.answer: Detection includes object locations as well as category predictions.
options: Detection only reports the file size.
Detection includes object locations as well as category predictions.

questions.question: What should match a pretrained vision model at inference?
questions.answer: The expected input channels, size handling, and normalization.
options: The expected input channels, size handling, and normalization.
Any arbitrary preprocessing because pretrained models are invariant to it.

questions.question: Why keep photos of one physical object in one data split?
questions.answer: Closely related images can otherwise make evaluation unrealistically easy.
options: Objects cannot be photographed more than once.
Closely related images can otherwise make evaluation unrealistically easy.

questions.question: How does a frozen feature extractor differ from full fine-tuning?
questions.answer: Its parameters stay fixed while a task-specific head can be trained.
options: Its parameters stay fixed while a task-specific head can be trained.
It retrains every parameter from random values.

questions.question: What is a useful robustness check for a camera classifier?
questions.answer: Evaluate different lighting and backgrounds representative of deployment.
options: Only repeat the same image many times.
Evaluate different lighting and backgrounds representative of deployment.

sources.title: PyTorch: transfer learning for computer vision

lessons.title: Introduction to NLP
lessons.description: Turn text into representations and evaluate language tasks carefully.
lessons.prerequisites: Python data handling and model evaluation.
objectives: Choose a text representation and baseline
Recognize leakage and language-specific failure cases
explanation: Natural language processing covers tasks such as classification, extraction, search, translation, and generation. Define what the output should contain and how correctness will be assessed. A short fixed-label classifier may be easier to validate than an unrestricted generated answer.

A bag-of-words representation counts terms while discarding most order. TF-IDF weights terms using their frequency within documents and across a corpus. Fit the vocabulary and any corpus statistics on training data. Contextual embeddings can capture richer patterns, but cost more and still need evaluation.

Preserve information deliberately. Removing punctuation, negation, or accents may change meaning. Evaluate languages, misspellings, long inputs, and ambiguous cases separately. Deduplicate templates and group related messages before splitting so near-identical text does not inflate held-out results.

terms.definition: Dividing text into units used by a representation.
The terms or tokens recognized by an encoding.
A text weighting scheme using term frequency and document frequency.

lessons.example: A support team labels messages billing, technical, or unclear. A term-count baseline is cheap to inspect. Include both “payment failed” and “payment did not fail” to reveal whether the representation loses a distinction that matters.
mistakes: Removing negation as an unimportant word.
Learning vocabulary from the final test set.
Assuming one language result applies to every language.
lessons.exercise: Write twelve invented support messages including ambiguity and negation. Define labels, a template-aware split, and a count-based baseline. Identify three cases where word order or context changes the correct label.

questions.question: What information does a basic bag-of-words representation mostly discard?
questions.answer: Word order, while retaining term occurrence information.
options: Word order, while retaining term occurrence information.
Every occurrence of every word.

questions.question: Where should a text vectorizer learn its vocabulary?
questions.answer: On the training partition before transforming evaluation data.
options: On every future test message first.
On the training partition before transforming evaluation data.

questions.question: Why might removing the word “not” damage a sentiment classifier?
questions.answer: Negation can reverse the meaning of the phrase being classified.
options: Negation can reverse the meaning of the phrase being classified.
All short words always increase sentiment accuracy.

questions.question: Does a contextual embedding eliminate the need for text evaluation?
questions.answer: No. It changes the representation but still has task and distribution limitations.
options: Yes, embeddings guarantee language understanding.
No. It changes the representation but still has task and distribution limitations.

questions.question: How should repeated support templates be split?
questions.answer: Group related or near-duplicate templates to reduce cross-split leakage.
options: Group related or near-duplicate templates to reduce cross-split leakage.
Place identical copies in both training and test sets.

lessons.title: How large language models work
lessons.description: Make sense of tokens, context windows, and next-token prediction.
objectives: Explain tokens and context budgets
Distinguish training from generation
explanation: A language model estimates likely continuations of a sequence. Text is converted into tokens, which can be words, pieces of words, or other units. During generation, the system repeatedly selects a next token based on the current context. This produces useful language, but likely text is not necessarily true text.

The context window limits how much tokenized information a model can handle in a request. Instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, and output allowances all compete for a budget under provider-specific rules. Longer context also creates practical cost and relevance trade-offs.

Training changes model parameters. Supplying a document in a prompt typically changes the information available for that request, not the model weights. This is why an assistant can discuss a newly supplied document without being retrained, and why you still need a retrieval or storage strategy for future requests.

terms.definition: A unit of encoded input or output.
The supported token capacity for a request under model-specific rules.
Numeric values learned during training.

lessons.example: Imagine a request budget of 8,000 tokens for a hypothetical model. Reserve 1,000 for output and 1,000 for instructions and history, leaving at most 6,000 for documents. Use the actual provider rules for a real model; this number is an exercise, not a product specification.
mistakes: Assuming one token equals one word.
Assuming a long conversation is remembered forever.
Treating prompt context as permanent training.
lessons.exercise: Design a context budget for a document assistant. Include instructions, history, passages, output, and a margin for tokenizer variation.

questions.question: Is one token always one word?
questions.answer: No. Token boundaries depend on the tokenizer, language, and content; a word can span several tokens.
options: No. Token boundaries depend on the tokenizer, language, and content; a word can span several tokens.
Yes, token counts equal word counts.

questions.question: Does adding a PDF to a prompt retrain the model?
questions.answer: Usually no. It supplies request context; updating model weights is a different process.
options: Yes, each prompt permanently changes the weights.
Usually no. It supplies request context; updating model weights is a different process.

questions.question: A request exceeds its context limit. What should you do?
questions.answer: Reduce or select the relevant input, summarize history carefully, and reserve output capacity according to model rules.
options: Reduce or select the relevant input, summarize history carefully, and reserve output capacity according to model rules.
Keep adding documents until the model remembers them.

questions.question: Why can next-token prediction produce false statements?
questions.answer: A plausible continuation can lack factual support. The generation objective alone does not verify external truth.
options: The model intentionally lies whenever it is uncertain.
A plausible continuation can lack factual support. The generation objective alone does not verify external truth.

questions.question: What should a context budget include?
questions.answer: Instructions, relevant history, retrieved material, and output allowance, with the exact accounting checked for the selected model.
options: Instructions, relevant history, retrieved material, and output allowance, with the exact accounting checked for the selected model.
Only the user’s latest sentence.

lessons.title: Sampling, hallucinations & grounded answers
lessons.description: Understand output variation and build a better evidence loop.
objectives: Separate variability from accuracy
Define an answerable and unanswerable test set
explanation: Generation can select tokens using different sampling settings. Temperature often changes how concentrated the token distribution is, while top-p limits candidates by cumulative probability. Support and interactions vary by model, so check its documentation before changing these settings.

Lower variability is useful for repeatable tasks, but it does not create knowledge. A model can consistently produce the same wrong answer. Reliability comes from a combination of relevant evidence, clear task boundaries, validation, and evaluation on realistic inputs.

For a grounded assistant, ask for claims supported by supplied documents and a clear response when evidence is missing. Verify that cited passages actually support each claim. Multimodal inputs add another layer: a blurry chart or ambiguous image may make a confident interpretation unsafe.

terms.definition: Selecting an output from a probability distribution.
Connecting an answer to supplied evidence.
Declining to answer when support is insufficient.

lessons.example: Give an assistant a two-paragraph return policy. Ask one covered question and one about an absent international policy. A useful system answers the first with a supporting passage and explicitly says the second is not covered.
mistakes: Using temperature zero as a truth guarantee.
Accepting a citation without checking its supporting text.
Forcing an answer to every question.
lessons.exercise: Write three answerable and three unanswerable questions for one document. Define what a good abstention should say.

questions.question: Does low temperature guarantee truth?
questions.answer: No. It can reduce variation in supported models, but a stable answer can still be factually wrong.
options: Yes, deterministic output is always factual.
No. It can reduce variation in supported models, but a stable answer can still be factually wrong.

questions.question: What makes a citation useful?
questions.answer: The cited passage must be accessible, relevant, and actually support the specific claim being made.
options: The cited passage must be accessible, relevant, and actually support the specific claim being made.
The citation only needs to look like a document title.

questions.question: A policy omits international returns. How should the assistant respond?
questions.answer: State that the supplied policy does not answer that question and offer an appropriate escalation route.
options: Invent a likely international rule.
State that the supplied policy does not answer that question and offer an appropriate escalation route.

questions.question: Why test unanswerable questions?
questions.answer: They reveal whether the system respects evidence boundaries and abstains instead of filling gaps with plausible text.
options: They reveal whether the system respects evidence boundaries and abstains instead of filling gaps with plausible text.
They are useful only for measuring typing speed.

questions.question: How should blurry image evidence be handled?
questions.answer: Acknowledge uncertainty and request a clearer source or human review when the interpretation affects the result.
options: Treat visual guesses as verified measurements.
Acknowledge uncertainty and request a clearer source or human review when the interpretation affects the result.

lessons.title: Inference: latency, batching and serving
lessons.description: Balance response time, throughput, and memory in a serving system.
objectives: Separate first-token and total latency
Explain the tradeoff between batching and interactive response time
explanation: Inference includes more than generating tokens. A request can wait in a queue, load model weights, process the input, and then generate output. Time to first token measures the initial wait; total latency measures completion. Throughput counts completed work per unit time.

Batching combines work to use hardware efficiently, but waiting to assemble a batch can delay individual requests. Longer contexts, more generated tokens, and concurrent requests also consume memory. A warm model avoids loading overhead at the cost of keeping resources occupied.

Measure under the expected workload instead of extrapolating from one short prompt. Include bursts, cancellations, timeouts, and long requests. Bound queues, apply backpressure, and separate interactive requests from offline jobs where useful. Record quality alongside speed when comparing quantization or smaller models.

terms.definition: Work completed per unit time.
Time from starting a request until the first generated token arrives.
Limiting incoming work when processing capacity is occupied.

lessons.example: An invented service finishes ten queued requests per second but makes a user wait eight seconds before seeing text. Adding workers might help, but first split queue time from generation time and check whether the workload fits memory.
mistakes: Reporting only tokens per second.
Increasing concurrency without measuring memory.
Treating a warm local benchmark as a cold-start production result.
lessons.exercise: Design a load-test table with concurrency 1, 4, and 8; short and long prompts; first-token latency; total latency; failure rate; and memory. State a queue limit and what users see when capacity is exhausted.

questions.question: Can high throughput coexist with poor interactive latency?
questions.answer: Yes. A system can finish much work while each request waits in a queue.
options: No, throughput and latency are the same metric.
Yes. A system can finish much work while each request waits in a queue.

questions.question: What does a cold-start benchmark include?
questions.answer: Initialization or model-loading work that an already warm process may avoid.
options: Initialization or model-loading work that an already warm process may avoid.
Only the final token generation step.

questions.question: A concurrency increase causes out-of-memory errors. What should you inspect?
questions.answer: Memory per request, context lengths, model residency, and queue limits.
options: Only the font size of the response.
Memory per request, context lengths, model residency, and queue limits.

questions.question: Why separate offline batches from interactive requests?
questions.answer: Their latency goals differ, and long batch work can delay interactive users.
options: Their latency goals differ, and long batch work can delay interactive users.
Batch work always uses no computing resources.

questions.question: What should accompany a faster-model benchmark?
questions.answer: Task quality and failure measurements under the same workload.
options: Only the new model name.
Task quality and failure measurements under the same workload.

lessons.title: Multimodal application design
lessons.description: Combine images and text while preserving evidence and uncertainty.
objectives: Choose a task-appropriate modality
Design checks for missing or unreadable evidence
explanation: A multimodal application processes more than one kind of input, such as text and images. Decide what each modality contributes. A product photo can show damage; a written description can supply context. Neither automatically establishes quantities, identity, or facts outside the visible evidence.

Check the selected model and API for supported modalities, file encodings, size limits, and output structure. Validate uploads before forwarding them. Keep the original evidence linked to extracted fields so a user can inspect the region or passage supporting an answer.

Evaluate failures specific to the inputs: blurry text, rotated images, missing pages, conflicting captions, or inaccessible audio. Give the system a way to report unknown rather than invent an observation. Treat instructions embedded inside images or documents as untrusted content, just as you would retrieved text.

terms.definition: A type of input or output, such as image, audio, or text.
Recognizing characters from an image.
Connecting an output claim to supporting input evidence.

lessons.example: A fictional receipt assistant extracts date, vendor, and total. A blurred total becomes “needs review” with the original crop attached. Arithmetic can check subtotal plus tax, but a consistent sum does not prove the printed numbers were read correctly.
mistakes: Assuming every text model accepts images.
Inferring hidden facts from a photograph.
Discarding source images immediately after extraction.
lessons.exercise: Describe five receipt inputs: clear, blurred, rotated, missing total, and conflicting text caption. Define expected outputs, review triggers, and which evidence a reviewer needs. Include one unknown result.

questions.question: Does a vision-capable model automatically support audio?
questions.answer: No. Check supported modalities for the selected model and endpoint.
options: No. Check supported modalities for the selected model and endpoint.
Yes, all multimodal models support every file type.

questions.question: What should accompany an extracted invoice total?
questions.answer: A reference to the supporting source region and a review state when unclear.
options: A claim that visual extraction can never fail.
A reference to the supporting source region and a review state when unclear.

questions.question: The amount in an image is unreadable. What should happen?
questions.answer: Return an explicit unknown or request clearer evidence instead of inventing a number.
options: Return an explicit unknown or request clearer evidence instead of inventing a number.
Choose a plausible amount from similar invoices.

questions.question: Why evaluate conflicting image and caption inputs?
questions.answer: They reveal how the application handles inconsistent evidence and possible manipulation.
options: Captions are always more authoritative than images.
They reveal how the application handles inconsistent evidence and possible manipulation.

questions.question: Is a matching arithmetic checksum proof of correct OCR?
questions.answer: No. Multiple misread values can still form a consistent sum.
options: No. Multiple misread values can still form a consistent sum.
Yes, arithmetic removes all recognition uncertainty.

lessons.title: Write prompts that actually work
lessons.description: Create clear instructions, useful examples, and testable outputs.
lessons.prerequisites: Basic familiarity with an AI assistant.
objectives: Specify task, context, constraints, and output
Compare prompts on the same examples
explanation: A prompt is a task specification. Tell the model what outcome you need, provide the information it should use, and describe a result that can be checked. Replace vague requests such as make this better with concrete criteria such as summarize the three decisions and preserve all dates.

Examples can clarify boundaries that prose leaves ambiguous. Include ordinary cases and a difficult edge case. Keep examples consistent with the instructions; a contradictory example teaches a competing pattern. Treat quoted documents as data, not as a source of new authority.

Prompt quality is an empirical question. Keep a small set of realistic inputs, define a scoring rule, and compare versions on the same cases. Record failures before rewriting. A longer prompt is justified only when it improves useful outcomes without unacceptable cost or fragility.

terms.definition: A requirement or boundary on the response.
An input-output example included in a prompt.
Explicit criteria for scoring a response.

lessons.example: Task: classify support messages as billing, technical, or unclear. Context: use only the message. Output: one label. Example: “I was charged twice” → billing. Boundary: if the message lacks enough information, output unclear.
mistakes: Adding conflicting instructions over time.
Testing only the prompt author’s favorite example.
Including sensitive data that the task does not need.
lessons.exercise: Write a three-label classifier prompt and six test messages. Include two ambiguous cases and define their expected outputs before testing.

questions.question: What improves a vague summarization prompt?
questions.answer: Specify the audience, facts to preserve, length, and output format so the result can be evaluated against explicit criteria.
options: Add more adjectives without defining success.
Specify the audience, facts to preserve, length, and output format so the result can be evaluated against explicit criteria.

questions.question: Why include an ambiguous example?
questions.answer: It demonstrates the desired boundary behavior, such as returning unclear instead of forcing an unsupported label.
options: It demonstrates the desired boundary behavior, such as returning unclear instead of forcing an unsupported label.
It guarantees every future ambiguity is solved.

questions.question: Two prompt versions use different test cases. Is the comparison fair?
questions.answer: Not reliably. Use the same representative cases and rubric so differences are attributable to the prompts.
options: Yes, any successful example proves superiority.
Not reliably. Use the same representative cases and rubric so differences are attributable to the prompts.

questions.question: What is a rubric in prompt testing?
questions.answer: A set of explicit criteria such as factual support, completeness, and format compliance used to score outputs consistently.
options: A set of explicit criteria such as factual support, completeness, and format compliance used to score outputs consistently.
A list of fashionable model names.

questions.question: Should a quoted email override the task instructions?
questions.answer: No. Treat it as task data; application permissions and validation must enforce the boundary as well.
options: Yes, the most recent text always has authority.
No. Treat it as task data; application permissions and validation must enforce the boundary as well.

lessons.title: Structured outputs & prompt testing
lessons.description: Turn model responses into data your application can validate.
lessons.prerequisites: Write prompts that actually work; basic JSON.
objectives: Separate syntax validation from business validation
Create failure cases for an extraction task
explanation: Applications need predictable data boundaries. A structured response might contain a category, a short explanation, and an optional date. Define field names, types, allowed values, and how missing information is represented. Use provider-supported schema constraints when available and still validate at the application boundary.

Valid JSON does not mean valid business data. A date may be a string yet be impossible or unsupported by the input. A numeric refund amount might be well formed but exceed the order total. Validate both structure and domain rules before performing any action.

Design a failure path before the happy path. Handle missing fields, refusals, truncated responses, unsupported inputs, and provider errors. A limited repair attempt may help, but never loop indefinitely or silently convert invalid data into a successful transaction.

terms.definition: A definition of allowed data structure and types.
A finite set of allowed values.
Checking whether data satisfies business rules.

lessons.example: Extract an invoice into {vendor, amount, currency}. Require a nonnegative numeric amount and a currency from your supported list. Compare extracted values with the source before approving payment. Missing values should trigger review, not invented defaults.

code.title: Validate business rules after parsing

mistakes: Calling JSON.parse and assuming all validation is complete.
Treating a schema as protection against unauthorized actions.
Retrying malformed output without a limit.
lessons.exercise: Design a schema for a meeting action item. Write invalid examples for a missing owner, unsupported date, and unexpected priority.

questions.question: Does parseable JSON prove an extraction is correct?
questions.answer: No. Parsing checks syntax; you must also validate schema, business rules, and support in the original input.
options: Yes, JSON syntax certifies factual accuracy.
No. Parsing checks syntax; you must also validate schema, business rules, and support in the original input.

questions.question: How should an unknown invoice amount be represented?
questions.answer: Use an explicit missing value or review state permitted by the schema instead of inventing a numeric amount.
options: Use an explicit missing value or review state permitted by the schema instead of inventing a numeric amount.
Use a plausible average invoice amount.

questions.question: The output says refund 900 for a 90 order. What next?
questions.answer: Reject or route it for review using business validation, even if the JSON and numeric type are valid.
options: Execute it because the schema accepts numbers.
Reject or route it for review using business validation, even if the JSON and numeric type are valid.

questions.question: Why limit output repair attempts?
questions.answer: A limit bounds latency and cost and ensures persistent failures become visible rather than an infinite loop.
options: A limit bounds latency and cost and ensures persistent failures become visible rather than an infinite loop.
Limits make schema validation unnecessary.

questions.question: What should an enum define?
questions.answer: The exact accepted values for a field, such as low, medium, and high, so downstream behavior is unambiguous.
options: Every possible natural-language synonym.
The exact accepted values for a field, such as low, medium, and high, so downstream behavior is unambiguous.

lessons.title: Adversarial prompt testing
lessons.description: Turn likely misuse and boundary failures into repeatable tests.
objectives: Write a threat-based prompt test set
Measure unsafe behavior and overblocking separately
explanation: Adversarial tests deliberately challenge the intended behavior of an application. Begin with a concrete boundary: confidential data must stay within its authorized audience, a classifier must use only allowed labels, or a tool must not act without approval. Define observable pass and fail conditions.

Use harmless synthetic cases covering conflicting instructions, long distracting input, malformed output requests, and instructions embedded in retrieved material. Add ordinary benign cases that resemble attacks so you can measure overblocking. Run the same cases against each prompt or model revision.

A passing set is evidence about tested cases, not a proof of immunity. Record the input, version, observed output, tool events, and reviewer rationale. When a failure is found, add a regression case and address the responsible application boundary; prompt wording alone may not fix it.

terms.definition: An input designed to challenge a system boundary.
Rejecting legitimate tasks while trying to prevent unsafe behavior.
A preserved example used to catch a returning failure.
